extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, and legal scholars (media/news-service litigation)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and factual criteria used in litigation over news misappropriation, injunctions, and the rights of news services to protect items (tips, local news, early-edition material) from competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to use material already published
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether we have the right to use material that had already been published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court frames this as a central legal question: once a story has been published (e.g., in early editions or on bulletin boards), how far can the original gatherer be protected from competitors taking and using that material? The transcript records skepticism about protecting material after it has been given to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of early editions/bulletin-board items (verification requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A news service may take information from early editions or bulletin boards only if it verifies the information from its own original sources and then issues its own rewrites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Jennings: 'they have a right to take it, provided they verify it for themselves, and then, from their own original sources, send out their own re-writes, send out their own dispatches.' The court contrasts copying verbatim vs independent verification and rewriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surreptitious copying of tips from another service's wire is improper
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking tips surreptitiously off another service's wire is wrongful and may defeat injunctive relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Jennings calls surreptitious taking 'surreptitious.' The Court states it would deny an injunction if both services routinely took tips surreptitiously from one another. The transcript treats covert tapping of another's wire as an improper practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Members' contractual obligation to furnish local news to their service
rubrics_metrics.description: A service's members are required by by-laws/contracts to furnish local news to that service and are prohibited from furnishing it to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Jennings repeatedly: 'our members are required by the by-laws to furnish us with local news... and they are prohibited from furnishing it to anybody else.' Breach of that obligation can be a basis for expulsion and possibly for injunctive relief against the recipient when it induces or benefits from the breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a trust/contractual relation can support injunctive protection
rubrics_metrics.description: When news is furnished to patrons under a trust relation or under a contract forbidding communication to others, courts may grant injunctions preventing competitors from using that information (sometimes for a limited period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The National Telegraph News case is cited: where the service was delivered under a distinct stipulation that it not be communicated to other distributing companies, the court granted an injunction (notably for sixty minutes after receipt) to prevent misuse. The presence and terms of such a contract/trust relation are pivotal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication vs private communication distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Material communicated privately to patrons under trust (not published) is treated differently from material published to the public; competitors cannot necessarily take private communications as they could published items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted headnote language: 'There was no publication, but merely a communication by the complainant to the parties occupying with it a trust relation.' The transcript emphasizes that publication to the public changes the availability of the information to competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal (limited) protection after receipt in special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases involving ticker/tape services given in trust, courts have awarded a short, fixed period of exclusive protection (e.g., sixty minutes) against competitors distributing the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transcript references a precedent where the court 'granted an injunction against the use of that for sixty minutes after it was received' to protect the complainant's patrons and prevent immediate redistribution to competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for positive proof to infer misuse (evidentiary requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff must present affirmative evidence from which the court can infer that the defendant used protected information; absent such proof, allegations are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Untermyer argues there is 'not a scintilla of proof that we ever used' certain machine-based information; the Court emphasizes applying law to the facts actually shown and the need for clear factual proof to support relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducement of breach vs mere purchase — need to show actionable conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a cause of action based on another paper's dealings (e.g., buying news or paying someone), the complainant must show that the defendant induced breach of contract or otherwise engaged in wrongful conduct, not merely that the defendant purchased a service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court and counsel debate whether buying news from the International News Service constitutes breach or actionable wrong to AP; Mr. Untermyer stresses that being a purchaser is different from being a party to the contract and may not give rise to the claimed cause of action without more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous practice vs isolated instances as basis for injunctive relief
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a pattern warranting injunction, plaintiffs should present multiple instances showing continuous practice, not just isolated happenings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Jennings says he put in 'enough... instances to establish continuous practice,' while defense counsel contends incidents come from only one branch office and are not proof of systemic practice. The court considers whether the affidavits sufficiently show an ongoing practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable remedies consider relative conduct (clean hands/unfairness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The propriety of injunctive relief depends on equitable considerations, including whether the plaintiff or the industry has engaged in similar disputed practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court suggests denying an injunction if it found that both parties engaged in the same surreptitious practice; the transcript repeatedly references industry customs and mutual conduct as relevant to equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperative association news (member-contributed) is protectable similar to agent-gathered news
rubrics_metrics.description: News contributed by members under cooperative arrangements is part of the association's news and entitled to the same protection as news gathered by the organization's own agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Jennings: 'in a co-operative organization... all of this news contributed by its members is just as much a part of the news of the co-operative organization, just as much entitled to protection as the news which the organization gets by its own agents.' Court discusses whether that creates a personal relation supporting injunction.
